take_homes: Groundedness only checks whether the output is true. A steering judge checks whether it's good, and I only have the first kind. I'll write one for the mails and reports our agents produce.
Keep the judge fixed, check its hash, and let only the generator's tactic file change. Otherwise the score is meaningless.
A flat score means the judge has run out of things it can see. I need to read the outputs myself and score the judge against my own verdicts.

monday.move: Put one existing agent output in an eval loop with a fixed judge and a tactic file, and hash the judge. First, hand-score ten outputs against the judge to see whether it agrees with me.
monday.who: Me, plus one engineer to wire it into our setup
monday.when: Monday morning for the first loop; the ten hand-scored outputs on Tuesday
monday.stop_condition: The judge agrees with my hand verdicts on about 8 of 10 and the flagged count stops dropping after round 3. If the judge misses things I'd have rejected, I fix the judge first.
monday.blocker: Nobody outside engineering has asked for this yet, and I haven't decided who maintains the judge files. I'll start with engineering outputs only.

misconception.why: I still think a strong agent gives good output. But I accept that I never checked whether my judge agrees with me, and that a clean score can hide a blind spot. I don't plan to review every output, only the judge, occasionally. The line about clean weeks eroding my ability to notice failures hit hardest.

one_line: The loop part is easy for anyone who already runs agents. What stuck was that a flat score tells you about the judge, not the work, and I haven't checked my judges against my own verdicts.
